speechtext:
Mr. WHITE (Leeds) moved that the House go into Committee of Supply.
Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.

There was an item reserved in Harbours and Rivers generally, an item for Quebec.
Quebec-harbours, rivers and bridges-general repairs and improvements, $60,000.

I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk) if the breakwater at Anse-au-Canard, Gaspe, for which an amount was voted in the estimates, will be built. I understand that tenders were invited some months ago for the construction of that breakwater and that, as appears by an answer given by the hon. gentleman to a question which I put some weeks ago, the tenderer had not made the necessary deposit, the tenders were, of course cancelled, new tenders were invited and on that second occasion the tender was considered too high for the department. Since that time nothing has been done. I received a letter to-day from a merchant of Newport, county of Gaspe, because Anse-au-Canard is one of the coves of Newport, and he states that he has learned on good authority that the work will hot be proceeded with. I would like to know from the hon. gentleman if any decision has been reached by the department in regard to that work. This is one of the public works in the county of Gaspe. I take an interest in 'those works Decause I have been somewhat associated with that county for fifteen years. There is another work in the county of Gaspe which does not appear in the list of items. I reier to the Gaspe landing pier. My hon. friend will remember that some three years ago a large amount was provided in the estimates for the construction of that pier, a contract was entered into with the firm of Dussauit of Levis or Quebec, I am not sure which. The work has been started and not seeing anything in the main estimates perhaps the hon. gentleman would let me know if it is his intention to place something in the supplementary estimates for this year? I may tell my hon. friend that Gaspe is the terminus of the Gaspe railway, better known as the Atlantic, Quebec and Western. The Atlantic Quebec and Western railway was started a few years ago. It runs from Paspebiac, or New Carlisle, for a distance of about 105 miles to Gaspe Basin. It is a first-class railway. It has been built at a cost to the company of a sum that is nearer $5,000,000 than $4,500,000. The company, in order to settle the railway position in the peninsula of Gaspe, has acquired the other railway, well known as the Atlantic and Lake Superior railway, so that to-day you have a continuous railway running from Metapedia on the Intercolonial railway as far as Gaspe Basin a distance of over 200 miles. The new company has made very substantia] repairs to
the old road and this coming year more repairs are provided for in its estimates. It has been the aim of the company from the beginning, and the hope of the people of Gaspe, to have a direct ocean connection between Gaspe and Liverpool or some port in Ireland. Steamers, if they were running between Liverpool and Gaspe, would, notwithstanding the claims of St. John, Halifax and Quebec, run by the shortest route, and, as regards the carriage of the mails, could afford a much better service to Canada than that which is at present provided. However, that is only for the future; let us see if, for the present, the government intends to build the landing pier at Gaspe. A large amount was provided for the construction of the landing pier. The Gaspe company intends to run its trains as far as the water's edge. Though I have no more political interest in my old constituency I yet look upon that work as a national work, at least as far as my native province is concerned. The peninsula of Gaspe is probably the first land that was sighted by the discoverers of Canada when first they came to the St. Lawrence river; in fact, looking at the archives the other day, I read a description of a trip made into the Bay of Gaspe by no less a traveller than Jacques Cartier himself. He called at a place well known in the country as Fontenelle. There he planted a cross and took possession of the soil in the name of God and the King of France. But this peninsula, although exceedingly wealthy in all sorts of resources, rich in timber, in minerals and in agriculture, has been tremendously neglected. That was due not so much to the fault of the governments of the day, although they were partly responsible for the state of affairs there, as to the existence of a company well known in the maritime provinces and on the coast of the Labradors. I refer to the Robin firm of Jersey.
This is a great company, which may in some-respects be compared to the Hudson's Bay Company. The Hudson's Bay Company were engaged in the pursuit of fur-bearing animals while the Robins were engaged in the fisheries of the Gulf of St. Lawrence. They have established in the gulf I do not know how many agencies. The oldest establishments are situated in the counties of Gaspe and Bonaventure. During the last 150 years they have extended considerably and now their stores and establishments are dotting the shores of the St. Lawrence river and the gulf. The Robins were anxious to keep the people to the fishing industry and they knew that the construction of a railway would perhaps induce the fishermen to go abroad and they have bitterly opposed, during half a century, the construction of any railway on that coast. I do not say that in disparagement of the

business methods of the Robins firm. They were, I suppose, working for No. 1. At the same time they prevented the people of Gaspe from getting their due in whatever government grants were given at the time for the expansion of the country. Gaspe is a very rich peninsula, and the construction of this railway will give the county an enormous development. The object of the company was undoubtedly to keep the people there and not allow them to go into any lumbering operations outside of the peninsula, in fact I do not think it is too strong to say they desired to keep them in a state of semislavery. In fact in 1896 when I was first elected for Gaspe, I travelled for many days along the 200 miles of coast in that county, and I found in many little places, in the little coves bordering the coast, old men and young men who had never seen the colour of a red cent in their lives. They were fishing and selling the fish to the Robin firm, receiving in return merchandise or goods. I obtained from the government of the day the establishment of a steamer service running between Montreal, Quebec and these various ports on the coast, in order to give a little more competition to the merchants in that far-away district. The result was most beneficial, but it was only the beginning. It was only when the construction of the railway was started that a new era dawned on the coast of Gaspe. The railway after many vicissitudes has been completed. It took about ten years of hard work on the part of the then member for the county of Gaspe to secure the completion of that road through federal and local subsidies.
My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley), decided upon a landing pier at the point called Sandy Beach. With his knowledge of _ the conditions in that section of the maritime provinces, he could appreciate the value and importance of that new feeder to the Intercolonial railway. In fact, the railway at Gaspe will, in the near future I arr. quite sure, through its connections with the Intercolonial railway, and at the boundary line with railways in the State of Maine, be an excellent railway for Canada and that section of the country as it will bring it into close touch with the United States, New Brunswick, and that part of the province of Quebec which is near the Gulf of St. Lawrence. This landing pier was decided upon at the terminus of the railway the contract was given, a large amount was voted, but the pier is not completed, and I see nothing in the estimates to complete it. I hope, however, that in the supplementary estimates the hon. gentleman will put in an amount sufficient to complete it, As I have said, I have no political affiliations with the county, I have only rov reminis-Mr. LEMIEUX.
cences to connect me with it, and they are of the happiest nature. Although I was defeated at the last general election, I bear no illwill to the electors of that constituency which supported me during 15 years. But I am very much interested in the completion of that railway, and I see in the completion of the landing pier, the termination of a work which I do not hesitate to qualify as one of national importance.
What is the length of file branch?

It is over 200 miles. It connects with the Intercolonial railway at Metapedia, at the point where the Intercolonial railway crosses the Restigouche river into Quebec. The first 100 miles were built many years ago, and the railroad was well known as the Baie des Chaleurs railway. Later, it passed to another company, and took the name of the Atlantic and Lake Superior railway. It was built as far as Paspebiac. The charter of the company gave it the right to build as far as Gaspe basin, 102 miles further, but as that first company at that time, was almost insolvent, I asked parliament to grant another charter to another company, which was known as the Atlantic and Lake Superior railwav company. This company built from the terminus of the old company, New Carlyle to Gaspe basin, has merged with the old, and it is now one trunk line running between Metapedia and Gaspe basin. The company has had many vicissitudes and for some time it was feared that it would stop its operations.
But fortunately the company is now in the hands of a strong organization in London, having at its head Lord Ranfurly, exGovernor of New Zealand, who came to Canada and inspected the road, and did not hesitate to take charge of the whole system. The company even this winter has been able to operate except for a few days, and I know, from the reports of the engineers in the Department of Railway and Canals, that it is a first-class railway. It was built by English engineers, and the only reproach to offer in regard to it is that it was built perhaps in a little too costly a way. At all events, it awaits only the completion of the landing pier at Sandy Beach in order to be fully equipped. I would like to know from the hon. gentleman if he has come to a decision in the matter, and if we may expect that there will be in the supplementary estimates an amount sufficient to complete the work.

I am anxious to give my hon. friend all the information possible in regard to the two questions he has put. The first has reference to the breakwater at Anse-au-Canard. The second question
FEBRUARY 9, 191a
has reference to the landing pier at Gaspe Basin at the terminus of the railway to which he has referred. Of course, it is more easy to explain the items for which credits are asked than to explain the reasons why the estimates submitted do not contain further items. However, I believe that my hon. friend has correctly stated what happened at Anse-au-Canard. Tenders were called for, and they were found to he too high. Other tenders have been called for, and I believe that the amounts of the tenders exceeded the amount claimed originally by the government for the execution of tire work. A number of works were projected, regarding which some calculations were made under the late government which are not to be found in these estimates. Naturally a new government coming in to exercise power under different circumstances and perhaps with a different view as to these different works, could not be expected to see absolutely eye to eye with the previous government in regard to each and every one of these works. I have mentioned on more than one occasion to the committee that we found ourselves confronted with I think larger demands than have ever been made in the past with respect to our principal shipping ports, our national ports, which were referred to at length in the reports of the Transportation Commission, dating back to 1903, and it has become to me evident, and it seems so to the government, that we must take steps without any delay to equip those national ports to meet present requirements. We are behind the times. We are far behind our American neighbours, in the equipment of our ports, and unless we make speedy preparation to secure the amount of trade to which we are legitimately entitled, we shall see that trade go gradually to the United States. AVe have found ourselves this year under the necessity of equipping with as great speed as possible our Atlantic ports, and the prospective opening of tihe Panama canal has made it necessary for us to prepare for considerable expenditure on our Pacific ports.
Nevertheless, in spite of these rather pressing requirements, the government is anxious to provide for local necessities as well, as far as that may be possible. As regards the peninsula of Gaspd, what my hon. friend has stated is perfectly true; and I may say that the hon. member who now represents the county of Gaspe, and who is I believe domiciled there, has brought to my attention on many occasions the needs of that county, which was to a certain extent unnecessary m my ease,' because I have had occasion to visit that important territory, and have become convinced by personal inspection and by much
that has been written of extreme interest with regard to its possibilities. There is room, we are told, within the Gaspe peninsula for over 50 thriving settlements still to be founded and developed; there are immense fisheries all around it; it has lumber wealth, mineral wealth, oil, and wealth of every other kind. The railway along the coast to which my hon. friend has referred will at least contribute to open up that peninsula. There is still the interior to be developed, however. The port of Gaspe is an important port, and there are other ports along that coast which it is claimed could be kept -open all winter. The landing pier at Gaspe Basin has certainly received the attention of the government, and I hope and expect to be able in the supplementary estimates to provide for the final execution of what work remains to be done. That will depend on what will be placed at the disposal of the department for the completion of those very important works which we desire to carry out as soon as practicable.

T think it is due to the committee that some explanation should be given why there is no item in the estimates for the purpose of completing this work, because a contract was let by myself as Minister of Public Works pursuant to the authority of parliament, a portion of the work has been done, and the contractor will be entitled to go on with the work and receive his pay. My hon. friend is aware that in these main estimates provision was made for all works which were under way, I think without exception.
My hon. friend's attention was called to one or two when these estimates were under consideration before, and he says that if they had been omitted through an oversight he would restore them in the supplementary estimates. In the estimates which he brought down, and which had been prepared by the late government, for the year ending 31st March, he included an amount of $87,500 for this wharf. Surely he ought to be able to tell us why that amount was left out, whether intentionally or by mistake. He has told us that the hon. member for Gaspe had called his attention frequently to the necessity of completing this wharf. Then why did he omit this item? As this work was under contract, he must recognize that the committee is entitled to some explanation.

If the facts are as my hon. friend has stated them, it is a case of omission, and will be provided for in the sup-plementaries. My hon. friend will admit, I suppose, that it is possible to make some omissions. In all cases of works under contract, my instructions were that they must be provided for.

The committee have some reason to complain with regard to the information the hon. minister is giving us concerning items that have been dropped from the estimates. I can quite understand that he cannot be prepared to give reasons why certain new works, that were never projected up to the present, are not provided for. But in the case of works which have been examined and reported on, and for the construction of which provision was made last year, we are entitled to some explanation. In my own province about two thirds of the whole estimates of last year have disappeared altogether from the present estimates. The House committed itself to the expenditure on these works on two several occasions. The late government laid these items before the House and got five-twelfths voted. Then the incoming government laid the same items before the House last December, and got the remaining seven-twelfths voted. In some cases tenders had been called for, but when we come now to examine the main estimates, brought down after recess, we find a great many of these items have disappeared altogether, and the minister does not appear to know why. I drew his attention on two occasions to the item of the extension of a breakwater at New Harbour in my own constituency, and have not yet been able to get any Teason why that item was dropped. I have no doubt that if the hon. minister would look into the reports and examine what his own engineers have said, he would not agree that this should have been struck from the estimates. That breakwater was started a great many years ago, it was built a part of the way out into the harbour. It became too small for the requirements of the people, the number of boats now fishing there could not be sheltered by the breakwater as it stands to-day, and an expenditure of $10,000 was voted last year for the purpose of extending that work. It is a very urgent work in my county. I have been asked by the people for some explanation why the item has been dropped, but have not been able to get any. In Nova Scotia out of $1,300,000, voted last year, two thirds of the whole has disappeared, and the minister does not explain why.

Is not the hon. gentleman losing sight of the fact that although these items appeared in the estimates last year they were not voted by this House? There were 400 docks in Nova Scotia which the House refused to vote.
These items I refer to were absolutely voted, all of them.
My hon. friend is an old parliamentarian, and I -would call his attention to the fact that we are Slightly ou.t-

side the subject under discussion We did not reserve any item from Quebec. We did reserve an item in Ontario for harbours and rivers in order to allow the members from that province to offer any observations they might judge fit. When the question was put with regard to Gaspe basin I thought it better to answer it, but the question which the hon. member for Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair) has put to me I have answered very often.
I do not think the hon. gentleman has answered it at all. He has given no reason why that item was struck from the estimates.

It seemed to me I have answered in the only way possible. It is not an argument to say that a public work has been reported on favourably by the departmental officer, that all, the preliminaries have been gone through and that the previous parliament voted an amount for the execution of that work. Parliament may approve of an appropriation, but if nothing was done with it, the new parliament can consider it as not having been utilized and can set aside that appropriation and vote another one. When the present government came into power there were a number of works in the estimates, five-twelfths of the amount for which had been voted, and the House will remember that the whole of the previous year's estimates were passed by parliament. That, however, did not entail on this government the necessity of carrying ou-t these works. Every year amounts are voted by parliament that are not expended, and those votes pass out of existence. It is absurd to pretend that at present the government is obliged to justify the leaving out of these works, the moneys for which bad been voted but never expended. What answer could I give my hon. friend. I could not explain to him what occurred in council when these particular items came up for discussion, if they were discussed at all. I can only give reasons for the appropriations that are submitted. It is quite open for any lion, member to criticize these estimates by comparison.
I submit that there is no special duty upon me at this stage to explain why previous appropriations that do not appear again in the estimates have been left out. That would be an impassible task. A number of these [DOT]appropriations being considered by the government, were set aside. New estimates have been placed before the House for other works deemed more necessary and urgent. While I am willing to give all the information at my command, I have not come here to explain why public works for which no appropriations are asked are not in the programme of the government.
[DOT]2793
I think my Ron. friend (Mr. Monk) does not quite recognize the rights of parliament in this matter. He seems to assume that whatever the government does is right.
By no means; I am too old in this business to have any such opinion as that.

See the extraordinary position in which the hon. gentleman places parliament. In the estimates which he submitted to this parliament, he asked for an appropriation for Nova. 'Scotia of $1,309,166. Hon. members may have voted for other public works throughout Canada, having in view that justice was being done by that province. (Because, after all, in endeavouring to discharge one's duty in connection with the estimates, one must have regard to the necessities and claims of the different provinces). The hon. minister will remember that, when he asked for the part of this vote of $1,309,166 not already voted, I called his attention to the fact that these were substantially the same items as had been submitted to parliament by the late government. He agreed. I said: We take it for granted that, speaking in the main, the government, in asking parliament for this vote, intends to go on with these works-of course, is not bound to go on with every item if subsequent reports should show that it was not necessary. We voted tire estimates on that understanding. That was the pledge made to parliament. Now he comes and, without rhyme or reason, reduces the vote for Nova Scotia from $1,309,166 to $445,000-leaves out two-thirds of the amount for which lie solemnly asked.
It looks like trifling with the House. Parliament would not have voted these amounts if it had supposed that the government had no intention of going on with the work, or if it had supposed that he was going to discriminate against in ova Scotia -and the same remai-k applies to my own province of New Brunswick, whose vote under this head is cut down from $800,000 to a little over $200,000, the total appropriations, including those on capital and on revenue account being reduced from $1,800,000 to $1,200,000. Has the hon. gentleman discovered that these works are unnecessary? Has he examined the reports of the engineers? It seems to me he is not discharging the duties he took upon himself when he said that the government recognized the utility of these works, and would proceed with them, and parliament voted the money.

The hon. gentleman's (Mr. Pugsley) memory I think is at fault. Those who were present at the time the seven-twelfths estimates were put through, will remember that they were put through without explanation, merely the balance of the year's estimates, and there was .scarcely any discussion. But even if matters were as the hon. gentleman has presented them, yet, the discussion of one year's estimates is entirely different from that of the following year. When these estimates were being prepared, the government was called upon to formulate its policy, if I may use that expression, with regard to each of these public works. I may say to my hon. friend, that if there have been any heart-burnings or omissions, the supplementary estimates will be found to be as satisfactory as possible.

I would like to have some better explanation from the Minister of Public Works than he has given. I am asked by the people in my county for an explanation of the omission of this item, and I have not been able to give it. I have to tell the people that the former government agreed to make that expenditure, also that the principle was agreed to by this parliament by voting the seven-twelfths of the appropriation last December; but. when I ask the minister why he has dropped the matter, I am only told that I must not ask such an absurd question. I hope the minister does not seriously mean that I am to tell the people that it is an absurd thing for me to ask why important items like this have been dropped. If I could persuade him to read the papers and go into the matter seriously, I would leave it to his own judgment whether he should not go on to complete these works. We have spent some $27,000 in connection with the protection of that harbour. It is in an exposed part of the coast and the completion of that harbour is much needed. If it is the policy of my hon. friend to build no public works in counties represented by Liberals, of course, there is no help for it, the work will have to remain unfinished. But I hope that when the supplementary estimates come down, we shall find that he has given censideration to the matter. But I would like him to give to-night some more satisfactory explanation than that which he has given.

There is not a single harbour in the country where the work is finally completed. The government is endeavouring to complete work in all the harbours as soon as possible. In the case to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sinclair) refers, the government has not seen its way clear to continue that work at the present moment. The reason that he supposes-that the counties represented by a member who is not friendly to the government are discriminated against has never entered my consideration.
But it happens, as my hon. friend knows, that appropriations are made for several * years and are not used. In cases where the

works were actually begun, we are continuing them. Where contracts were made we are keeping faith with the contractor.
Does the hon. gentleman say that if a different result had happened in Guysborough, and a supporter of the government had been sent here, he would have struck that item out of the estimates?

I can tell my hon. friend that at the present moment members on this side of the House are complaining that we have struck a number of items out of the estimates which concern their counties, and which were in previous estimates.

I may tell my hon. friend that not only will there be one railway having its terminus at Gaspe, but there is another railway which is now under construction, partly in the county of Rimouski, and partly in the county of Gaspe.	There is a railway which was
started a few years ago at St. Flavie, and has now reached Matane in the county of Rimouski, and from Matane I understand it is the intention of the company, a very substantial company, to build to the village .of Cap Chats, and as far as Gaspe Basin. I think it is the intention of the company to have a port at Mont Louis which at all times of the year is an open harbour, according to statements made by navigators of experience. Then from Mont Louis this railway would join the main line of the Atlantic, Quebec and Lake Superior, using the Atlantic pier as a terminus. The port of Gaspe is an open port at least nine months and a half during the year. In seven seasons out of ten Gaspe is open the whole year round, practically it is open all winter. I do not know what is the case this year, but I have known ships sailing to and fro from the port of Gaspe several months after December. I wish also to refer to another matter connected with the terminus. The late government had granted a certain amount for the construction of a road leading towards the terminus on the coast. If my hon. friend will look at the map of Gaspe he will see that the coast is indented, and the largest indentation is at Gaspe where the arm of the sea practically divides the peninsula in two. Now this bras de mer prevents the people on the other side from reaching the railway, and they have to go a long distance before they reach the landing pier. The population on that side of the peninsula is not so large as on the other side, but it is quite large. The road which was provided by the ex-Minister of Public Works gave to the people of that section of the peninsula a commodious route, which enabled them to reach the landing pier. I understand that work was started some months ago. I know the sen-Mr. MONK.
timents of my colleague from Gaspe on that subject, and I specially commended this work to his care after the election. I hope my hon. friend will take note of that fact. The road which starts at Ste. Ma-jorique, and goes towards its terminus, is of great importance to the people there, and one might say that it is part and parcel of the terminus.

My hon. friend the sitting member for that constituency has pointed out to me the necessity for terminating these works, and has done so with so much insistence that I am afraid that, out of sheer exhaustion, I shall have to give way.

From the discussion we have had, and the explanations the minister has given on these items in the estimates prepared by the late government and afterwards approved by this government, but which he has dropped, it would seem to be a fair inference that the present government were not disposed to give any promise of the performance of these works at a later date. But the minister has held out a hope that when the supplementary estimates come down a great many of these appropriations asked for at the present time, and that were in the estimates last year, will likely re-ap-pear. But he has not explained why these items were allowed to drop after receiving the approval of this parliament some months ago. If it were not proper that these appropriations should have been made, then when the minister prepared his estimates he should have had before him information which would justify him in dropping such as were not retained, and he should have had the reports of his engineers as to the works that were of a pressing character. I can understand that in the old estimates, there were votes for new works of which, under the circumstances, he might feel constrained to delay tlie construction until a later period. But where these appropriations were for repairs, for works begun but not completed, and he had his reports to that effect, and the man who prepared the estimates for him saw the necessity of going on with these works, as is evidenced by 'the fact that they appeared in his estimates, I say it is up to the minister to explain why he dropped them. My hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) has suggested that if the minister would take the House more freely into his confidence, and would tell us which of these dropped in the estimates last year he proposed to have in the sup-plementaries, then we would be able to get along much faster.
A great deal of the discussion could be avoided and time saved, if the minister would tell us what he proposes to do with regard to these -works. In the county which

I have the honour to represent, there are over a dozen works, for which appropriations were made in last year's estimates, in some cases for the maintenance of works already constructed and in others for slight extensions to make the works of service to the community. All of these items, with the exception of two, have been dropped. They are not new works. There are a number of other works that I asked the department to have attended to, which are new works. The minister could very well say that these could not be attended to this year. But these works, to which I refer, were provided for in the estimates last year, and they were approved of by members on the other side of the House, when they agreed to vote seven-twelfths of the amounts appropriated for them a couple of months ago when last year's estimates were voted on. If the minister would explain that he intends to bring down these items in the supplementary estimates the grievance would be remedied. When last this matter was up for consideration, I asked him if these items would he in the estimates, but he evaded my question. I think that my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) is quite right in stating that we have not yet been able to get from the minister such information as we are entitled to. The minister states that to reply to our question would necessitate him telling us what took place in council. Surely he does not mean to tell us that in council, when these items were up for consid-deration, he was told:	You will have to
cut out these items in Nova Scotia in order thal the national ports shall receive proper treatment. Surely he is not going to confess that he was weak enough to surrender and leave out these items which are of such vital interest to the fishermen and other residents of the county which I represent. The Minister of Militia can get all the appropriations he wants. 1 observe that he finds no difficulty in getting the large appropriations which he demands. Yet, these little works in the province of Nova Scotia are neglected. To some hon. gentlemen on the other side these may seem of very little importance. It is quite right that the national ports should be attended to, but look at the conditions along the shores of Nova Scotia. A great many of these places are distant from the railway, from 20 to 50 miles, the means of communication they have is by water, and they require these little wharfs and breakwaters along the shore which some of_ our friends opposite have in the past minimized. I remember that the hon. member for Montreal, St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), used to have a set of photographs, of works in the maritime provinces. I do not know where they came from, but, they were supposed to represent some of the harbours and coves down in Nova Scotia.
Most of them were the figments of his own imagination, I have no doubt. He held . them up to ridicule, but these hon. gentlemen opposite minimize the importance of these works along the shores of Nova Scotia, because they were trifling in cost. Is that a reason why the minister should drop them or fail to see that they are provided for? Thirty-four thousand dollars was voted the year before last for works in the county which I have the honour to represent, a good many of which items were revotes of the year before that. It is only a very trifling amount, yet it covers a dozen different places and it means convenience and accommodation for hundreds and hundreds of people, a great many of whom are engaged in the fishing industry and it accommodates others who have to use these ports for the purpose of transportation. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the minister should frankly answer the question which had been put to him. I read a list of places when this matter was up the last time, for which appropriations are desired and he promised to take the matter into his consideration and give me an answer.
I have heard nothing since. My hon. friend from Guysborough has done likewise. If the minister would tell us frankly that these items are dropped because he did not want to allow the late government to get credit in the country for providing 'thf se works and that he intended to provide for them later on when the supplementary estimates came on so that somebody else might get the credit for having secured these works a great deal of our anxiety will have been ended.

My hon. friend offers a very great temptation. If I can tell him that I have provided for the public works of his county in the supplementary estimates ihe work of the committee will be much shortened. I know what that means but I am afraid I must resist the temptation. I cannot at this moment tell my hon. friend what provisions will be made in the supplementary estimates. Nor is it relevant to the present discussion. I could not do it under any circumstances.
I have told my hon. friend also several times since these estimates were under consideration, when I was asked in regard to leaving out public works in the county of Inverness, that my hon. friend refused to name a superintendent of worxs. I have a memorandum in my office which I will bring here for a number of these works where the district engineer reported that, although the amount had been voted by parliament, and he had applied to the sitting member for a superintendent of works, he had refused to give any answer.
It is not the county of Inverness that I have the honour to represent. It is a much better county-the county of Antigonish.

My hon. friend will pardon me; I am not as familiar with Nova Scotia as he is There are several instances where the district engineer thought the sitting member did not find the work important enough to indicate to him a superintendent of works. I give that as an instance why the minister might naturally conclude that the work is not necessary.

I think the minister has got the two counties confounded. As far as Antigonish is concerned you cannot produce any evidence from the district engineer or anybody else of the fact that I refused to name a foreman.
I think it is Mr. Bernas-coni who is the district engineer.
No, he is at North Sydney, Cape Breton. Mr. Millidge is the district engineer there.

I will look up the memorandum. I was under the impression that although he had applied for a superintendent of these works he had teceived no nomination. However, that is not the main point at issue. Where works were begun, where there was any aontract, where there was an obligation upon the government to carry out the engagements of the previous administration, these works have been provided for, or they will be in the supplementary estimate's. They have to be provided for because the government is not free; it has to keep faith. But, where the whole matter was open, I submit to the committee that the government was free to prepare its estimates as it thought fit, just the same as the government is free to prepare its estimates without reference to the estimates of the year before. The government is perfectly at liberty to follow the estimates of the previous year or to change them. It is a new operation every year. The minister must be prepared to justify those items for which he asks a credit from parliament. It must be evident that the 'whole discussion of a previous debate cannot be reopened at this stage.

The minister has conveyed the impression that the failure in going ahead with these works was due to my neglect in not complying with the request to name a clerk of works. I give that information which he has received the most emphatic contra diction. In no case did I refuse to name Mr. MONK,
a clerk of works with perhaps one exception. He referred the other evening to the Mc-Ara's Creek work and said that the engineer had asked me to name a clerk of works. Perhaps that is correct, but the reason was that only five-twelfths of the money was available and it would be useless to start the work with only five-twelfths of the amount required on hand.
The work would be stopped when the money was exhausted and the five-twelfths might be wasted. I refused to name a foreman, in that particular case, and that case alone. Then too it was on the eve of an election, and I did not think it was the right thing to start these works then, it would be said they were being use for election purposes, and the county of Antigonish is not susceptible to that kind of influence, and cannot be brought to support the government by the refusal of public works. The people are not built that way, they are too independent for that.

My hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Murphy) is not here to-night, and he wished to speak upon a work in Ontario. Could it be arranged that on any item an hon. member might be allowed to speak about this Ontario work?
Certainly.

I wrote a note to the minister informing him that I desired information about a number of small works in my county. The minister has just said that he is not very familiar with the geography of Nova Scotia. The county which I represent has not a large population, but it has a tremendous coast line, perhaps as as long as any other county in Canada, so we have quite a number of small works such as wharfs and breakwaters. The first *section of the coast extends from the head of East bay to the Grand Narrows, and then you follow along the sea coast to North Sydney. On the other side of the Bras d'Or lakes there is another 75 miles of sea coast, all in my county. There is a large island in the centre of the Bras-d'Or lakes with a coast line of 70 miles, and there is the regular Atlantic sea coast of 150 miles. All of these stretches of sea coast are fishing grounds, and all are more or less exposed to the terrors of the Atlantic ocean. The minister will thus understand why we seek the opening of larger harbours to enable our people to go out and fish and return to shore with some degree of safety. Breakwaters have been built during the last 15 years at a number of places along the shore. Before their construction the only boat the fishermen could use was such a boat as could be hauled up over the beach away from the surf in the evening, shoved out in the morning and reballasted. Since the construction of the breakwaters they have been able to use fairly good sized

schooners, and in many instances gasolene boats which take shelter in some of the little harbours we have made, or behind the breakwaters. I am sorry that I haYe the same complaint as other members from Nova Scotia that many works which have been started are dropped out altogether. For instance the wharf at East bay, which is almost finished, built by day work and to cost only $4,000, cannot be utilized as it requires a little further work. Then at Rose Point an old wharf built under the Macdonald government requires repairs, the material was on the ground, but it has been left out of the estimates. I cannot believe that Mr. Bernasconi, the chief engineer in that pai;t of the country, would report that works which were halfway finished should be dropped.
I picked out the items for which the *money was voted in the estimates of last year, and I sent the list to the minister on the 6th of February, and I will ask that the attention of himself and of his officials be given to these works, and that he will at least proceed with those which have already been begun. The most important work on my list is the opening of the harbour at Aspey bay. That is in a section of the country where there is no available harbour at present. There is what is called a harbour, but the water is not deep enough. It is a magnificent fishing place in a good agricultural section of the country, which is within easy reach of the large markets at Sydney, North Sydney and Sydney Mines; and if the people could only get in touch with the steamer which passes their doors every day but cannot go in, it would be a great benefit to them. For the last 30 years there has been an agitation for the opening of this harbour. This could be accomplished simply by cutting through the bar, which would enable the steamer to go to a splendid harbour inside, 6 miles long and a mile and a half wide. At low water there is at present sometimes not more than 6 feet, and it is impossible for steamers to go in. Last year I prevailed on the late Minister of Public Works to put $50,000 in the estimates to make a start on this work; everything was in readiness for the calling of tenders, and I was told that tenders were called; but I was afterwards informed that some slight changes in the plans were necessary before the work could be put under contract, I find that this work has been dropped altogether from the present estimates. If nothing else were done in my county, I would ask the hon. minister to give some consideration to that work, as it is of the most vital importance to that section of the country. His officials will tell him that ft is supported by all the influences which both 89	.
sides of politics in the county could bring to bear; every public body in the county has sent petitions for it, which are on file in the department. Therefore, I hope that when the supplementary estimates are brought down something will be provided for that work. Even if I had to sacrifice every dollar for other public works in the county, I would be to a certain extent pleased if- provision were made for the opening of that harbour.

I wish to draw the attention of the minister to a few very necessary public works in my county, in the hope that he will provide for them when he makes up the supplementary estimates. The first is the extension of the breakwater at Charlos' Cove. The breakwater there has been partly built, but it is not long enough to be a proper shelter for boats as it stands at present. It requires to be extended about 150 feet or more. A considerable sum of money has been spent upon it, and it is a very important work in that locality. Another work is the dredging of the Tittle at Canso. This is a narrow channel connecting Chedabuc-to Bay with Canso harbour. It makes a short cut for the fishermen in stormy weather, but it requires some dredging. Orders were given, I understand, last year that this should be done, but owing to the confusion connected with the election and the difficulty of finding any one to undertake the work, it was not carried out. It would only require a very small expenditure. Then, there is an application for the dredging of St. Mary's river, which my hon. friend will find on the files of the department. This is a very important river, as it the only means of communication with the sea for a large district. It is a lumber district, and the logs are floated down the river and are sawn at Sherbrooke; but the river is not deep enough to enable steamers to come up. Some dredging has been done in the river in the last few years, and there is urgent need that it should be continued. Also the breakwater at Lower Half Island Cove on Che-dabucto bay is another important work. The dredging of Guysborough harbour is another. There is a bar at the mouth of the harbour, and it is filling up to same extent, and something will have to be done to make the harbour suitable foT the purpose of navigation. My hon. friend will remember that the branch railway that was to be built in that county was struck off, in the slaughter which was made in the estimates, and unless we can get these harbours dredged so as to afford some communication with the sea, it will be very difficult for our people to carry on their business at all. There should also be a small appropriation for cutting a channel at Port Shoreham to



enable the fishermen to get shelter. A few hundred dollars would be sufficient for that. If the minister will examine the applications for these works which he will find on his files and deal with them when he brings down the supplementary estimates, I shall be very much obliged.

I desire to call the attention of the minister to some works which are similarly situated in the county I represent. For the breakwater at Little Anse, provision was made at the last session of parliament, and tenders were called for, and the contract awarded during the month of September last. I would like to call the attention of the minister to that item particularly as the timber has been purchased by the contractor, and I hope he will not lose sight of it when he comes to prepare the supplementary estimates, There were also provided for breakwaters at Port Richmond and Charlos Forest Cove, a wharf at Louisdale and a wharf at For-chu. Tenders were called last year for the construction of these works, 'but I am in formed that contracts have not been entered into up to the present time.
These works are all equally important and I would urge on the hon. minister that he should give attention to them in his supplementary estimates. There are repairs to breakwater at Petit die Grat which are urgently required. This is an important public work which was built years ago, but it is to-day in such a condition as to make the expenditure of public money on it absolutely necessary. The same remark applies to the wharf at Poulamond, which is in very bad condition indeed, and for which an appropriation of $1,600 was voted last session. The objection which the hon. minister raised in connection with the public work asked for by the hon. member for Antigonish (Mr. Chisholm), namely, that he refused to recommend a clerk of works, does not apply in this instance. A clerk of works was appointed a year ago, and I trust that these repairs will be made at the earliest possible opportunity. If the hon. minister will look at the estimates voted in the beginning of the session, he will observe that amounts were appropriated for other public works in my county which I shall not now enumerate, tout I would a.sk that he would give some attention to these in his supplementary estimates, so that the people living in these localities may reasonably expect that in the not distant future these very necessary works will be constructed. I desire to impress upon him the fact that these expenditures are asked for solely because they are absolutely required and because the works in question are very important. If he will refer to the reports of nis district engineer, he will learn, that he has testified to the urgency Mr. SINCLAIR.
and necessity of these works being carried out.
Mi* CLARK (North Bruce). I hope that lion, gentlemen opposite do not imagine for a moment that they have a monopoly of grievances against the Minister of Public Works and the government generally with regard to public works in the various constituencies. I hope they do not imagine . that items have been struck from the estimates of the Public Works. Department merely because the counties interested happen to have returned members supporting the opposition. Hon. gentlemen on this side, myself among the number, have grievances of a similar .nature against the minister and the government. I do not think we are making complaints; but if hon. gentlemen opposite are going to file their orders for items in the -supplementary estimates, then hon. gentlemen on this side should do the same. We have had the hon. gentlemen rising and filing their claims in this public way on the Minister of Public Works and insisting that he shall place these claims in the supple-men-t-aries; and if he is going to do that for his opponents, I insist that he should also do it for his friends.
I shall be very glad to think that he draws no distinction between his friends and his opponents in the matter of appropriations for public works. -

It is rather a new departure to find hon. gentlemen opposite taking that line. I wonder if my hon. friend remembers how the Minister of Public Works in the late government (Mr. Pugsley) acted when he met with demands for public works from those who were not in sympathy with him in his public policy. I remember when he was quite ready to give a public building to a county adjoining mine in a place not very important and where the population was small, but -absolutely refused to spend a dollar in th-e adjoining constituency.
What about Aylmer?

That is not in the county of Halton. I am speaking for my own county, and I remember well the ground the -hon. gentleman took m the last Session of parliament when he refused any explanation in the county I represent. I then told him that the people of my county were not beggars, that the Liberal party was not going to remain in power for all time, and that we were willing to wait. I did not know that I was such a good prophet, but we did wait and I hope that my representations will have a little more effect on the present Minister of Public Works than they had on the previous one. At any rate it will not be my fault if I ' do not succeed. I was pleased to hear the

hon. gentleman who spoke before me saying that he wanted the government to give their attention to both sides indiscriminately, but that is a new policy for the Liberal party.

I wish to say a few words to press on the Minister of Public Works the claims of the county I represent. I think it is the duty of hon. members to place before the government the requirements of their various counties, and in my opinion any one who fails to do so is not performing, as he should, his duty to his constituency. I do not think that anybody in this House has .a right to hold his tongue in such matters. I perhaps have been doing a little too much of that during the last two or three years, and I now propose, when I have something to submit to the government, to urge it openly in committee. I may say that I have implicit faith in the desire of the hon. minister to treat every county properly; and now that he is preparing his supplementaries, I have some suggestions to submit to him with regard to requirements in my county which no doubt will receive fair treatment. There are several works in the county of Inverness which I would like to see provided for, if possible, in the supple-mentaries. They were all provided for in the supplementaries of last year. I wish briefly to enumerate these works. I shall take first the work at Tory Harbour. That is an artificial harbour, which was provided for in the supplementaries of last year. It is an important harbour, intended to afford shelter for perhaps some 40 or 50 fishing boats. There are some forty or fifty families depending on the fishing industry here. If the hon minister will look over the reports of his engineer, he will see that the expenditure on this harbour is one which the engineer declares absolutely necessary and urgently called for. Then there is Long Point wharf. That wharf was built five or six years ago, but is now practically of no use as it is almost covered with sand, and it. is necessary to extend it out some 200 feet if it is to be of any benefit to the people. I need not enumerate the various reasons why these works should be attended to, as the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) has gone over that ground already and the same conditions) obtain in my county as in his. Then there is Crignish where a wharf is urgently needed. The lumber has already been bought for this work, and I am sure, from what the hon. minister has told us, he will see that the necessary amount will be provided in the supplementary estimates to carry on this work.
I now come to Mabou Harbour which is another important work, as the hon. minister will see if he looks up the engineer's report. It is the only harbour in that part of the county, which is very 89 A
prosperous and has large exports, and where this channel protection and dredging is urgently required. At Finlay Point, there is another wharf which is now practically of no use. That wharf requires to be extended some 200 feet, as the minister will see by the report in his department. Then there is Margaree Harbour where a sheer dam is required, and I would lay particular stress on the importance of this work, because that is the only harbour in the stretch of country some 40 miles in extent with a population of some 17,000 or 18,000 people. $10,000 was appropriated last year for the purpose of I'uilding a sheer dam there.
The minister will see, by reference to the report of the engineer, the importance of this work, and will understand that it should be continued as soon as possible. Then, there is a little harbour, the Friar's Head harbour, which is for fishing boats. It was partly built four or five years ago. The amount necessary to finish this harbour is not large, and I am sure that when the hon. minister knows the number of fishermen there, he will see the importance of completing it. There are over 50 fishermen depending on this harbour for boat protection. Then we come to Cheticamp Point. When I tell the minister that from this point over two hundred fishermen go out to the fishing grounds, and that a settlement of something like three hundred families depend for a living here on the fishing industry, which is (depending upon the shelter of this breakwater, he will see the importance of it. I might spend half an hour enumerating the various necessities for this work, but it is not necessary, as the hon. minister has the report of the engineer before him. There is a work at Pleasant Bay, also, an extension of the wharf that is there now. The wharf is of no use unless extended by building another breakwater to the northeast. There is a thriving settlement here of over 40 families who depend on fishing for a livelihood and this wharf is the only protection the fishermen have. Then we come to Marble Mountain. The minister has a report on this work and he will see thereby the importance of this work also._ I simply place the demands of the county before the minister that he may provide for them in the supplementary estimates. I have always found the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk), courteous, and I hope he will see his way to grant our reasonable demands. AM these 'grants are contained in last year's estimates.

I am glad to hear suggestions; but I corroborate what has been said by hon. members on this side, that it is a great mistake to imagine that claims and complaints come only from the otheT side.
I have had quite a number of complaints

on this side of the House. I may say we have a heavy budget, I suppose $30,000,000 when all is considered, but four or five hundreds of millions would not suffice to build all the public works asked for of the department. The hon. gentleman must not forget that during all the years we were in opposition we got very little from the government. I was fifteen years a member of the House and never got a single public work, except on one occasion, when I asked the Minister of Public Works of that time for a small w'harf. He said he would give the wharf, provided I would not speak about it in the House. I do not say that that is the right way to obtain public works, but you might try' it.

I was struck with the faith of my hon. friend behind me {Mr. Win. idhishotan) who .said that he had no idea that counties would be discriminated . against that were represented by opponents of the government. In reply to what has been .said by my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk), I might say that the experience of which they spoke was that of my own county during eighteen years of Conservative rule, with the exception of four years when the county was represented by a Conservative. During those four years a few public works were built along the coast. It was not that the requirements of the county were not brought before the government, because Mr. John A. Kirk and Mr. D. C. Fraser, .who represented the .county, urged the government year after year to do some-about the .coast of that county. But during fourteen years, the name of the county, or any place in the county, does not appear, I venture to say, in the estimates. On one occasion a Minister of Public Works came to the shire town of any county and told the people in plain language that the only v-ay for them to get appropriations for the county was to vote Tory-[DOT] support the government and you will get something.' That was the doctrine. I hope we have improved since then. I could give many instances to show that under the late government that did not prevail. For example, the late government was asked to do .something for the construction of branch lines in eastern Nova Scotia. They looked over the ground and found a hundred and fifty miles of that country without a railway. Half was in the county of Halifax, represented at that time bv the leader of the present government and Mr. Crosby, two Conservatives, and the other half was in Guysborough, represented by myself. They laid down two branches .of railway one for each county and put. about . $1,000,000 for each in the estimates. And what did the present government do? When they came into power they struck the pen through the ap-

propriation for Guysborough and left^ the appropriation for the county of Halifax. That leads me to fear that my hon. friend behind me has too much laith in the present administration, and also that the hope expressed by my hon. friend from Inverness (Mr. Chisholm) may not be realized. But you cannot starve or drive the people of Guysborough into supporting the Tory party.
Oh, oh.

You may try it, but you cannot do it. During fourteen years when Hie Conservatives ruled before, it wras tried and it did not work and it will not work now. I .should like to feel that this was not_ going to be the policy of the present administration. But, apparently it is to'be their policy. They are doing the same in the case of officials, cutting off heads everywhere in order to give jobs to their friends. They are even cancelling mail contracts, taking advantage of a clause in each contract which enables them to cancel. We know that the prices will go up for the carrying of mails. Owing to the greater expense of living, the higher price of horses, &c., it is certain that when they let the mail contracts they will have to pay for them. But they are cancelling these contracts merely to give them to their friends.

Did the hon. member (Mr. Sinclair) really take seriously the votes for his county in the estimates last year, made on the eve of an election? Did the hon. gentleman really think that the government were going to spend that million dollars in his riding?

I don't think there is any necessity to answer a question like that. My hon. friend knows very well that the late government always took these matters seriously. They not only put items in the estimates, but they spent them. If the present government will carry out the policy of' the late government, it will be the best thing they can do for themselves and for the country.
I would Lke to ask the hon. gentleman how his county fared during the regime of the Liberal party?
Fairly well.

Well, tell us all about it. My impression is that the hon. gentleman has got so much that there is scarcely any room for any thing more. Where would he put any more public works in his comity after fifteen years expenditure by the government he was supporting?

The hon. gent'eman is quite right, the late government treated

my county much better than ever it was treated before. But the great requirement in my constituency for its development was a branch railway, and it was a great disappointment to the people when the present government was returned to power, because they felt that this important worn that had been started by the late government might be stopped, and that fear has been realized.

It is a well-known fact that this branch railway in the hon. gentleman's riding always appeared during the regime of the Liberal party just on the eve of an election, and it has never been built yet. I am sure that if the Liberal party were in office again, every time an election came round there would be an item in the estimates for this railway down in Guysborough. The hon. gentleman should have grafted the plum tree with the plums on it, he should have had that railway built before there was any chance of an election.

The hon. gentleman knows as well as I do that the question of branch lines was only decided on last year, and there was no time lost after the government committed themselves to the policy of building branch lines to the Intercolonial. Immediately on that announcement being made, the supplementary estimates were brought down with a million dollars for Guysborough county, and engineers were placed at once on the work to get ready for construction. There was not a day lost by the 'late government in regard to that matter. The statement of my hon. friend that this road has been used by the Liberal party for election purposes I absolutely deny. The people in my constituency have been endeavouring for many years to get the government committed to this work before they were finally successful. The contracts that were made with the different companies were not made at the time of an election, but between elections. Hon. gentlemen opposite had better not talk too much about election promises. Let me remind them that their leader, w'hen he went out west last summer promised the people everything that was in sight, promised to give them back their natural resources, to give them back their mines, their lands; and coming down to the head of Lake Superior, he promised terminal elevators at the public expense, promised chilled meat refrigerators out in the west when there appeared to be no public demand for them. I need not go over them all. On the very eve of the local election in Prince Edward Island he sent a telegram down to the Conservative party in Prince Edward Island, saying that he was going to build a car ferry across the strait,
and to widen the gauge of the road, in order to help them to win the local elections. Why, Sir, on the eve of the election he issued a manifesto to the fishermen of the maritime provinces promising that he would give them free medicine. There was nothing he could think of that he did not promise in order to get votes. There was never anything known like it in the history of Canada. Hon. gentleman had better not talk coo much about pre-election promises.

I am a little surprised at hearing the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) complain that estimates brought down by the late government previous to the elections have not been renewed. As a matter of fact it is known to every person in the province of Nova Scotia that, during the last fifteen years, public works have always been dangled before the constituencies just on the eve of an election. -The hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) made a similar complaint a little while ago. The hon. gentleman himself was a member of a provincial legislature for some years, which, just previous to the general elections, made a declaration that this road was going to be built; 1 went through his county in 1905 and I found that men were actually at wOTk with wheelbarrows, building that road. As the hon. gentleman has spoken of my constituency, it is only fair

that I should not take his observation with silence. The statement that he made in respect to public works in the county of Richmond only being commenced on the eve of' an election is absolutely untrue

I know something about the Lennox passage bridge.

The Lennox passage bridge was an incident merely between the provincial government and the municipal council. The municipal council of Richmond passed a resolution in 1903 by which they undertook to contribute $25,000 towards a bridge across Lennox passage if the provincial government would spend $25,000 as well. The provincial government accepted that proposition and made all reasonable speed in the preparations for the construction of that bridge. After the work had been commenced the municipal council met and rescinded their resolution. When they did that the local government felt that they were absolved from carrying out their part of the undertaking and the work lapsed. So much for my hon. friend's story. The hon. gentleman has been drawing a distinction between the conduct of the Liberal government and the Conservative party in the matter of public works. I remember that in 1891, upon the eve of an election, the then Minister of Public Works in the Conservative government, went into the county of Guysborough and, speaking in the shire town, told them in plain language that unless Guysborough returned a Conservative to the House of Commons, there would he no public money spent in that constituency.
With respect to public works in my county, 1 would say to you, Mr. Chairman, that the late Mackenzie government, in 1877, const meted a breakwater in the district of L'Ardoise at a cost of $30,000. In the course of time repairs were needed upon that breakwater, but the county was represented by a Liberal and the Con-* servative government absolutely refused to spend one dollar for repairing the breakwater much less to expend money upon new public works. fishermen it became a menace to them and it was not until the breakwater had been absolutely destroyed that an appropriation was finally made to renew it and it cost the late Liberal government twice as much to rebuild that breakwater as it would have cost if the late Conservative government had spent a reasonable amount each year in maintaining it. What part of the Athabaska river is it intended to improve?

At Grand Rapids, amongst other smaller rapids. The work was started in 1911-12, blasting rock in an endeavour to improve navigation. The amount of rock blasted it is impossible to estimate as much of the work was done through the ice, and the measurement could not be taken. River pilots claim great improvements in the rapids this spring, buit a large number of rocks still need to be removed.

The amount asked for the coming year is somewhat less than for the .current year. I want to impress the importance of the improvement of the Athabasca river and the amount of good that may be done by a moderate expenditure for that whole northern country. The whole country that constitutes the basin of the Mackenzie river, 1,500 miles from north to south, by about 500 from east to west, nearly one sixth the total area of Canada, is available to the navigation of this river and its tributaries. River , navigation is reached at Athabasca Landing by a branch of the Canadian Northern now about completed. There is then river navigation from that point to the Arctic ocean with the exception of the rapids of which my friend has spoken, and another serious rapid at Fort Smith. It would be impossible to improve the Tapid at Fort Smith, but the Grand and a succession of rapids below are quite capable of improvement to such a degree as to permit navigation by loaded scows down stream very freely.
My criticism would be that the amount asked by the minister is small for the purpose, and that a moderate expenditure there would be of immense benefit in developing that northern country. Until these recent improvements were made at Grand Rapids, all scows going down the river had to be unloaded and the goods had to be portaged from the head to the foot of the rapids, the scows being taken down light through the rapids or brought out of the wafer and carried on a tramway. By the improvement already made it is possible to run the loaded scows through the rapids, without portaging, but there still remains a great deal to be done to make it reasonably safe.
It is now possible, but it is not safe, and a reasonable further expenditure would make the rapid, while not absolutely safe, so improved that there would be no extra charge on the goods by reason of their being taken over the Grand Rapids, whereas at present the extra charge amounts to something like 50 cents per hundred pounds. Below the Grand Rapids is a succession of rapids extending to Fort McMurray. In a distance of about 80 miles there are six or eight rapids, each one of which requires some improvement to make it safe for the

passage of scows. Scows do run down now without discharging except at the Big Cascade. In low water they have to discharge part of their cargo, which adds greatly to the cost of freight and the risk of navigation. I am informed that it is practical to improve both the Big and the Little Cascades, so that the scows can run through full at low water. I would urge the minister to make additional provision in the supplementary estimates to carry on the work which has already been begun.
The reason why it is more desirable now to push these improvements than it was before, is because, rail communication having been established with the navigation of the river, the great impediment that formerly existed to the transport of heavy machinery and supplies is done away with. Until the railway was built to the Landing all goods had to be transported by wagon or sleigh, and only comparatively small pieces could be taken; but now the largest and heaviest machinery can be taken. A great deal of money is being invested in the attempt to develop petroleum wells on the Athabasca below these rapids, a very large quantity of machinery was taken down last summer, and there is no doubt a great deal more will go down in future years, particularly if a successful strike is made. The expenditure already made has been of great advantage, but I would urge- the hon. minister to increase the amount so that substantial work can be done that will afford an open channel for loaded scows down these rapids, so that they can carry the heaviest machinery necessary for the development 'of the mines and the wells without unloading at the rapids and without danger of destruction.

Last summer an incident took place at Vercheres, which I might perhaps recall to the memory of the minister. The government of the day, and especially the Postmaster General were taken to task because, forsooth, the Postmaster General did not furnish to the postmasters of Quebec signs for their post offices in the French language. The Postmaster General is not obliged to furnish signs in paper or in enamel, or in wood to any of the postmasters, yet there was great excitement in the province of Quebec, the Postmaster General was a very bad man indeed, he was a traitor to his language because he did not furnish to the postmasters of Quebec signs in French to distribute all over the post offices.
