Then I desire to call the attention of the minister to a Canadian artist, of the name of Mrs. Hamilton, whose family happens to come from my constituency. She had an exhibit at Wilson's here a couple of weeks ago. Her paintings have been on exhibition in Paris, and she has been recognized there and all through Europe. She has also been recognized in Canada to the extent that the Duchess of Connaught has purchased several of her paintings. Therefore, I think that this government should see that her work is represented in the National Gallery, and also somewhere in these buildings. There is no doubt about her ability and the splendid work she has done. I ask the minister to investigate her work and give her the place to which she is entitled as a Canadian artist.
I certainly will do so. I am glad my hon. friend has called my attention to her work, and I will bring his observations to the attention of the Advisory Board.
Will the minister tell us who the Advisory Board are?

Sir Edmund Walker, president of the Canadian Bank of Commerce; Dr. Shepherd of Montreal, who is quite an authority on matters of art, and the Hon. Senator Boyer.
Construction of water storage dams and regulation works on the upper Ottawa river and tributaries, $200,000.
Will my hon. friend inform the committee how this will be expended?
For the continuation of the works already undertaken-the Timiska-ming darn, the Quinze dam and the Kip-awa dam.
What is the condition of the work on the Timiskaming dam?
The department is continuing the work by day labour under careful supervision.

The reason I ask the question is this. I have noticed in some of the Conservative newspapers reports of information supposed to have been given to them by the commission which this government has appointed-I refer to the commission of which Mr. Morine is the chairman, and the other members of which are Mi. Lake and Mr. Ducharme; a commission which is sometimes spoken of as an impartial commission, consisting of two defeated Conservative candidates, and the president of * Le Devoir,' a strong partisan newspaper. Now, I object very strongly to this commission giving out partial information with regard to any Mr. MONK.
matter they are investigating, until all the evidence has been heard, and all the facts can be submitted to the public. I have read what purports to be a statement which they must have given out to the _ Conservative press in which these allegations are made; That, in the first place, the work was let without tender; that it was changed to a concrete dam; that no tenders were called for the concrete work; that afterwards the contract was again changed and the contractors received great favours. One might infer from these statements that the contractors were still going on with the work and were to receive the sum of $350,000. Now, I can imagine nothing more unfair than for these one-sided statements to go to the public. I have no objection whatever to all the facts connected with any public work with which I as Minister had anything to do, being made public; but what I do object to is that a commission shall give to a section of the press, to the newspapers supporting the government, a one-sided story, and not all the facts of the case. With regard to the Timiskaming dam, the facts are simply these. Tenders were called some years ago for a dam to be built partly of timber and partly of concrete. After "the tenders were received it was decided. to make a change in the plans and construct the dam entirely of concrete. Members of the committee know that during the last few years there has been a great change in the views of engineers as to the desirability of constructing works of this character as far as possible wholly of concrete. Concrete is rapidly taking the place of timber in the construction of dams as well as many other works. So far from the contractors not being the lowest tender on concrete, they were the lowest. The tenders were called on the unit plan, so much per cubic foot for timber work, and so much per cubic foot for concrete work. They happened to be the lowest tenderers as the matter was figured out by the engineers of the department. When it was decided to change the work and make it wholly of concrete, the work was given to the contractors, who were the lowest on concrete work as well as on the dam as originally planned.
It is not from newspaper reports supposed to be given out by the commissioners that I am speaking. Not one step was taken except upon the report of the responsible engineers of the department. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works has very properly born testimony himself to the very great experience, good judgment and the devotion to the public interest of these gentlemen. Not a step -was taken by me in connection with the Timiskaming dam except upon the report of the responsible engineers of the department. When

it was suggested to make the work entirely of concrete, the contract was given to the lowest tenderers and they proceeded with the work. I believe a change was made in the site of the dam. Hon. gentlemen know that there is no more difficult work coming within the purview of engineers than subaqueous work, as it is difficult to ascertain with accuracy the nature of the soil under water. A slight change was made in the location, with the result tnat there was a vast deal more unwatering to be done than had been figured up by the engineers. After that was brought to the attei tion of the engineers and myself as minister it was decided that, under all the circumstances, it would be reasonable to allow the contractors the actual cost of unwatering, doing it on the force system- that is adding 15 per cent to the actual cost and paying that to the contractors. Subsequently there was an unprecedented pressure owing to the spring freshets and the coffer dam, which the contractors had built, at great expense, was carried away. That gave rise to a dispute between the contractors and the department. The contractors contended that by reason of the change of site, they had encountered quicksand and there were enormous difficulties which they had not anticipated. The matter was gone into fully by the engineers. On more than one occasion Mr. Coutlee, who has charge of the work, was sent to make a careful examination, and the result of his inquiry was that the engineers recommended it would be better for the department to release the contractors, to take the work out of their hands, and proceed to complete it by day labour; and it was agreed that the contractors should be paid exactly what they had expended on the work-not one dollar more. They were not to be allowed any profits but simply their actual outlay, the amount to be determined by the experts of the department. That was done, the department proceeded by daywork, and the government of the day has carried out that plan. That is the whole story with respect to the Timiska-ming dam. Yet these commissioners have allowed to go out to the public the impression that some great fraud has been committed on the public by the contractors with the connivance of the department. I thought it my duty to state the facts, and I took occasion some time ago to move for the papers, and I shall be glad if any hon. member will take the trouble to go through the papers, which will verify every word I have said. This matter gave me great anxiety. I was careful to take no step except after the most careful examination by the engineers of the department, in whose judgment, integrity and regard for the public interest I had the greatest confidence after four years experience; and
my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, after his experience of four months in the work they are carrying on, has the same confidence in these gentlemen which my four years experience taught me to place in them. I wish to repeat that I took no step of any kind or description in the matter, and gave no order except upon their recommendation.

If my non. friend the ex-Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) expects any justice from these hon. gentlemen he will be sadly disappointed. _ As regards the personnel of the commission, I know very well our late colleague Mr. Lake. I know that he was a very bitter partisan when he sat in this House, but he is certainly a gentleman. As regards Mr. Morine, I know nothing about him except that he was a defeated Conservative candidate twice, I think, in the maritime provinces. But I happen to know Mr. Dueharme by reputation. He is a citizen of Montreal, and one of the bitterest opponents of the late government that one could find in that city and district. He is president of the company, which publishes ' Le Devoir,' the organ of the Minister of Public Works. He is also president of the company which publishes ' Le Nationalists,' a Sunday paper, which has been condemned, I do not know how many times, by our courts for libel, not only against private citizens but against the judiciary. Two of the editors of that paper were sent to jail for their gross^ libels against the judiciary of the province of Quebec. While Mr. Dueharme of course found at all times the means of avoiding costs and responsibility, we know that he is the financial backer of those who are publishing that sheet, If I were to be investigated officially as head of a department by Mr. Dueharme, I would strongly object for many reasons which my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works knows very well. Mr. Dueharme, besides being strongly biased politically, has had a very notorious career in Montreal. My hon. friend knows that for a few weeks he was president of La Banque Provinciale and was forced to resign because the shareholders would not have him any longer as president, and he has ceased to be a member of the board of directors.
Was he a defaulter, and what reasons does the hon. gentleman assign for making these very serious charges that will go out to the public against this gentleman who is not here to defend himself?

I shall bring shortly before the House the facts in connection with that case. Mr. Dueharme was obliged to resign as president of La Banque Provin-

dale, a position he occupied for a few weeks only.
He was also secretary of the municipality of Ste. Cunegonde, a suburb of Montreal, for some years. People know what has been his success in that capacity. I say he has a very notorious reputation [DOT]in Montreal, and the country surrounding Montreal; and I would certainly refuse to be investigated by Mr. Ducharme. I think he rather needs investigating himself than to be engaged in investigating others. I repeat to the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), that he cannot expect justice from Mr. Ducharme. He is there as a party man to render services to liis party, to do the muckraking work and nothing else.
He is likely to find plenty of muck to go into.
Perhaps, if he could go into any hon. friend's (Mr. Bennett) constituency, he might find lots of muck.
He will find lots of it in that riding in the acts of friends of the late government.

The hon. gentleman has only to denounce them and bring them to the bar of the House, or if they are in this House to name them. I am not afraid to tell Mr. Ducharme that I would refuse to be judged by him, for he has been judged by the citizens of Montreal, by the shareholders of La Banque Provincial and by the people of Ste. Cunegonde, who know what he is.

Nobody will find fault with the ex-Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) for claiming that his own administration of the department was a proper one. But I am surprised to hear a man of his experience attribute to members of the commission reports published in the papers, which I am perfectly sure could not have emanated from any of these commissioners. How these things get into the papers we do not know.
That report which I saw, stated that this was information which the commissioners had discovered.

It cannot be. Nor is there ground, very often, unfortunately, for the statements ' made by newspapers. It is quite conceivable that newspapermen may have had access to the .report of the Auditor General, which report if I am not mistaken, went at length into this Timis-kaming dam matter. I remember, long before this government came into power, correspondence given at some length, with comments of the Auditor General, in the report of the officer in regard to these contracts and the way the works were carried on. There alone, so fax as I know, the newspapermen could have found informa-Mr. LEMIEUX.
tion. I do not think my hon. friend has any justification for the aspersions he has cast upon this commission. The commission is composed of honourable men of high position, chosen amongst many by the government, not for the purpose of discovering anything against ex-ministers, but to endeavour to place all our departments upon -a proper footing and to make suggestions which would enable the government to improve many branches of the public service that are now defective. I take the responsibility as a member of the government, of having insisted that the appointment of this icommission was necessary fox that purpose, and I asked particularly that it should enlighten me with suggestions for the best administration of mv own department, a most important one. Was there no room for improvement? Will my hon. friend, or will any man -who has looked into the system, say that our dredging as it has been carried' on, is not susceptible of improvement ? - without thereby reflecting on any officer of the department or anybody else. Short though the time is during which I have had charge of the department, it has been long enough for me to learn that not only in the branch ocf dredging, but in other branches as well, improvements are possible and desirable. I have great hopes that when these men, who have leisure, who have business ability, have looked through my own department, they will be able to make most useful suggestions.
My hon friend (Mr. Lemieux) finds fault with the nomination of Mr. Ducharme. I very much regret this. Not that I feel it necessary to defend Mr. Ducharme in any way, 1 can assure the committee of that, his name not being as well known outside of my native province as it is there. I took the responsibility of suggesting his name as a man who has worked his way up in life and bears an honourable name where he is known. A man of wide means, a capitalist and a man of great business ability, I felt that if our province was represented on that commission-which I thought advisable-it should be properly represented by a not only able, but honest man, one holding a high financial position as a man of business. I am confident that, if his health- he is a man. of weak health-enables him to remain there, he will amply fulfil the expectations I have foimed. The hon. member for Rouville says that he is a director of - a newspaper, ' Le Devoir.' Why, I am interested myself in that newspaper. A number of us in Mont- eal have contributed, as far as we could, each according to his own limited means-Mr. Ducharme more than myself, because he has more means-towards the foundation of a newspaper, utterly, absolutely inde-

pendent, not under the control of anybody but its editor. That newspaper has rendered service in cur municipal elections. It is not, so far as I know, affiliated with any party.
Except the Tory party.

The hon. gentleman is very much mistaken. He must see evidence of absence of such affiliation in the paper every day I think the ex-Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) is mistaken in the view lie has taken of the commission. It is not a muck-raking commission, though it may, in its investigations, find out things that are not commendable. The prime object of its creation was to look through the departments and find out what improvements could be brought about. We have had several commissions which have produced good results. There was one of which Mr. Fyshe was president. Another was that of Judge Cassells. And I am convinced that the present commission also will produce good results. I think it would be better for the ex-Minister of Public Works not to anticipate what the conclusion will be. These' commissioners are not charged with a partisan investigation. - They are going to look into the administrative lepartments, and I do not see what reason there is to find fault with them beforehand.

What I saw in the papers did not profess to be what was contained in the Auditor General's Report. I have no objection to every word s^3Jed in that report being published.
What this professed t-o state was certain discoveries which this commission had made; it professed to be information coming directly from the commission.
What I object to is that partial information, one-sided information, half the truth mixed with considerable falsehood, should go to the public as being the true facts of the case. The public naturally look to a commission, particularly that portion of the public which does not know the partisan character of this commission, for the true facts in the case.

Has my hon. friend any
evidence that these statements were made by the commissioners to newspaper men, because I am sure they were not.

I simply judge from what I saw in reputable Conservative newspapers, which gave the impression that these were discoveries which the commissioners had made. Now I do not complain, notwithstanding the character of these commissioners, of a full and complete investigation of the department while I had the honour to preside over it, and I suppose 90
my hon. friend would not complain of a full investigation of the department while he presides over it. But would not my hon. friend expect to be treated fairly in such an investigation; would he not expect a full and complete investigation, before any factsi should be given to the public with respect to any particular case? No one reading what I saw in the newspapers purporting to come from these commissioners, would imagine for a moment that this work, under the circumstances I have indicated, was taken off the hands of the contractors on the recommendation of the engineers of the department. Their reports are all on file, but you would not imagine from reading this newspaper report that these commissioners had been able to find a single report of the engineers.
Would' it not be better to let that item stand until there is a larger attendance of members of the committee?
I have waited patiently to get the remaining estimates for my department through, and I expect to be extremely busy next week with preparing the sup-plementaries.

The hon. Minister of Public Works must not expect to escape criticism as to the character of the commission he has appointed. He says he expects to put his department on a better working foundation, and to establish a better system of bookkeeping in the department, inside and outside. If that is to be brought about, it cannot be brought about by novices who know nothing about that business. If there is to be an improvement in dredging, for instance, we want a man who has some knowledge of mechanics, who has some knowledge of building and operating dredges, engines and machinery generally. I submit that there is no qualification along any of those lines in the gentlemen of this commission. Mr. Morine and another gentleman who was at one time a member of this House, have no qualifications along those lines. Mr. Morine is a very estimable lawyer, a very clever lawyer, and if the Minister of Public Works wanted anything along the line of the profession of that gentleman, it would be well done. But when he asks him, who is only a lawyer, to take in hand the establishment of a new system of bookkeeping for instance, he is taking a man who does not know the first thing about doubles entry bookkeeping, a man who could not close a system of books to save his life.
I would suggest to my hon. friend that there will be an item in the supplementary estimates for the expenses of this commission, and perhaps it would be better to defer criticism until then.

I have nothing to say against these gentlemen along their own lines. But when he asks us to provide money to pay this commission, we would expect them to be men with a reputation in the direction of the purpose for which he has appointed them.

The Minister of Public Works has mentioned to-night what he has said before during the session, that he expects these men to give him some idea how to improve the dredging system now in vogue. Is my hon. friend serious in that? Are there more than two ways in in which you can do dredging, one by contract by the cubic yard by scow measurement, the other by cubic yard in situ? Will the hon. gentleman suggest any other way except those two ways in which to make improvement?

I would ask my hon. friend not to insist upon such an explanation at this moment. He has mentioned a measurement in place and a scow measurement. Without going further than that, does he think that the scow measurement that has prevailed in the past on our dredging contracts, instead of the place measurement, has been productive of good results? Does he advocate a continuance of the system of scow measurement as it exists to-day? I would ask the hon. gentleman not to enter upon that chapter this evening, because the hour is late. When the expenses of this commission come up at a later day, we will have an estimate for dredging in the supplementaries, and I will be prepared to go fully into that question, and to prove to the hon. gentleman that there are advantageous changes to be made in our dredging system.
Where are the commissioners sitting at present?

I believe they are sitting in the Canada Life Building at the present moment. They have merely begun their labours, I do not think they have investigated any branch fully.
Mr. LEMIEUX Will their central office be in Montreal or Ottawa?

In Ottawa.
Mr. LEMIEUX I ask, because I have seen Mr. Ducharme lobbying in the House, and I thought he had an office in this building.
I suppose a man may come up to the parliament building for other purposes than lobbying.
Why does my hon. friend think that Mr. Morine, a lawyer formerly of Newfoundland, and latterly of Toronto, could give him any assistance in

dredging? Does he think that Mr. Lake, a gentleman who came out from England, and engaged in farming at Qu'Appelle, in Saskatchewan, could give him any assistance in dredging? Does he think Mr. Ducharme-
Surely my hon. friend is joking.

Surely it is the engineers of the department who can tell my hon. friend best how to let these contracts for dredging. Of course, when contractors are guilty of fraud and inspectors lie in with them and try to defraud the government that is something that has to be carefully watched. But, my hon. friend does not require Mr. Morine, or Mr. Lake, or Mr. Ducharme to tell him that. My hon. friend knows that he has to employ honest officials and honest engineers. There are only two ways in which you can give out dredging work, one being to measure in the scow, and the other to measure in situ. It depends upon circumstances as to which is the better way to let the work. In some places, like canals, you can better let it by the contents in situ. In harbours, where you cannot get at the quantity very well in situ, you must let it by the quantity as per scow measurement. If my hon. friend will be good enough to bring down the papers relating to the Timiskaming dam before the supplementary estimates are brought down it will answer all my purposes.

Yes, they will be brought down at once. I cannot allow to go unchallenged what my hon. friend has said as to whether a lawyer is a proper judge of dredging. Of course a commission of that kind has the power of hearing not only engineers of experience but men who are absolutely conversant with the dredging business. Had this commission not been constituted I intended inviting to an examination of this branch of my department the well known firm of Price, Waterhouse & Co. who have looked into these transactions, and have an immense experience of them. It is not the fact that Mr. Morine is a lawyer, or Mr. Lake, a former English civil engineer, and now a farmer, or Mr. Ducharme, a financial agent, that impairs in any way their judgment when they have conducted their investigation in a proper way and looked into these transactions. But, we will have this matter up for discussion again.
Quebec harbour-improvements ait mouth of River St. Charles estuary-to complete contract, $66,000.
Would my hon. friend explain that item?
These are the large wharfs that are being built at present, Mr. Dus-sault has the contract.
Is it not for damming the St. Lawrence?

No, it is for building the large piers in the estuary of the river.
Quebec harbour-River St. Charles-improvements to navigation, $500,000.
What is that for?

This is a revote. We have not decided exactly the character of these improvements. The matter will be taken up as soon as parliament has adopted the estimates. I think the plan which consists in providing a dam and lock at that point is the one which seems to commend itself most to the people of Quebec. It is at present under the consideration of the engineer. Nothing has been determined.

Is it the intention of the government to have some of the large ports declared to be national ports? I know it was a very eloquent theme of my hon. friend when he was on this side of the House. I thought that as his estimates were eoming up he would refresh his memory by the report of the commission which was appointed and which was presided over by Mr. Reford. The conclusions of that report were that a bold and aggressive policy should be adopted by the government, that national ports should be declared and associated with that recommendation was the suggestion that such ports as St. John, Halifax, Montreal and Quebec should be declared to be free ports. I think I went so far as to suggest that Gaspe be a national port, but at all events my hon. friend was very sanguine about it, and on several occasions in the House he advocated that as being a sound policy. Would my hon; friend say now, or later on, whether he is going to take a decision this year or wait until another year about declaring national ports?

My hon. friend recalls a position which I took and which I maintain to the present day. I think that the report to which my hon. friend has alluded is the ablest report we have had on the transportation question since the matter has been under study in this country. The conclusions were admirable. National ports were recommended on the Atlantic, the Pacific, and the Great Lakes and these ports really exist at the present time. They do not require my weak voice to proclaim them national ports. They are national ports. They require our attention and 1 think my hon. friend sees in these estimates some evidence that they are receiving ^ recognition. We are approaching a realization of the dreams that I dreamed when in opposition.
But my hon. friend does not say which are free national ports.
Paris was not built in a day.
I know that; nor Rome.
Does calling a port a national port mean that it shall be a free port?
I think it ought to mean that, but it is not yet accomplished.
A national port is a good sounding name and we have lots of excellent ports on the Atlantic. I would like to know the rule by which the government decides that a certain port is a national port.

There is no strict meaning, we have used that expression since the report, of Mr. Reford and his colleagues, because in that report they recommend that certain of our ports be declared national and free ports and treated as such, national in this sense that the country shall undertake all the necessary expenditure to equip them. There were I think 11, Vancouver, Victoria, Prince Rupert, the Great Lake ports, Depot Harbour, Midland, Montreal, Quebec, St. John and Halifax. They were to be not only national ports but free ports as much as possible. My hon. friend knows that Antwerp and Liverpool and Bristol are national in that sense but they are not absolutely free ports. The commission was of the opinion that they should be made absolutely free. Whether we will be able to realize that or not I cannot say.
For the present the hon. gentleman is simply following the footsteps of his predecessor. He has not initiated any new policy.
Oh yes<.
In what respect?

My bon. friend was rather taking credit for doing something that we had not done, claiming that the government were making a new departure. Let us see how. He speaks of national ports at Port Arthur and Fort William. We appropriated for thes/e ports last year $1,050,000 while my hon. friend is this year asking only $1,000,000.
Wait till you see our supple-mentaries.
Then take Quebec harbour, we asked $625,000 and there is only $500,000 this year, and all of that is a revote.
You did nothing.
Yes we spent $625,000 last year.
Does he say that some real improvements were carried out in Quebec on any fixed plan?

Yes, we built a pier, 1,450 feet long, right along the shore of the St. Lawrence, where we have 40 feet of water, large enough to accommodate steamers bigger than any now on the Atlantic. We built a ' T ' for that wharf, and we were making improvements inside on the St Charles' river, doing a lot of dredging and giving very great additional accommodation. My hon. friend is simply carrying out improvements started by the late government. The only increase of any consequence, is in the cases of Victoria and Vancouver, where he is putting in $500,000. We were doing this out of the dredging vote, but he is treating them as national harbours, and changing the amounts to capital account instead of paying them out of consolidated revenue.
My hon. friend forgets that in the race for business, the harbour of Montreal defeated her great rival New York during several seasons.
In what business?
In ihe grain trade and butter and cheese.
The figures would be edifying.
It is due to the excellent adminstration of the harbour of Montreal by the three commissioners, who, fortunately, were not under the thumb of the Minister of Public Works.
I must take exception to that statement. These men are friends of mine, and I would not like that statement to go abroad.
He said they were not under your thumb.
And I never pretended they were.

They are under the direction of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and it -is due to their ability and efforts that the harbour of Montreal has been made such a great success. When my hon. friend said that our harbours are not equipped, surely he does not speak for Montreal.
Does the hon. gentleman say Montreal is properly equipped now?

As far as circumstances allow it is as well equipped as any other port in the world. Of course we are proceeding now to spend a large amount. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries is introducing legislation to lend more money to the Harbour Commissioners- of Montreal, I expect that within a short time the harbour of Montreal will be unexcelled on the continent of America. So far it has been so well administered and equipped, that we have been able in two or three years, in succession, to beat the record of New York.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. MONK moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will be taken up on Monday?
The Grain Bill and the other government Bills, and then Supply.
